faq.a: ORS replaces fluid and electrolytes safely, avoids IV complications, and can be given at the bedside.
faq.q: Why is oral rehydration preferred over IV in mild cases?

faq.a: Only for dysentery, suspected invasive bacterial infection, or confirmed parasitic disease; routine use in viral gastroenteritis is harmful.
Zinc reduces duration and severity of diarrhoea and improves immune function; it is recommended for all children over 6 months.

exam: A 10‑month‑old presents with 4 days of watery diarrhoea and mild dehydration. What is your immediate management plan? — Assess dehydration, start ORS 75 ml/kg over 4 h, give zinc, monitor weight.

A child with HIV on ART develops chronic watery diarrhoea. Which investigations are most useful? — Stool microscopy/antigen for opportunistic pathogens, CD4 count, consider cryptosporidiosis; if unavailable, treat empirically for common parasites.
How do you differentiate Shigella dysentery from viral gastroenteritis clinically? — Presence of blood/mucus in stool, high fever >38.5 °C, abdominal cramps, possible leukocytosis.
Why is azithromycin preferred over fluoroquinolones for paediatric dysentery? — Azithromycin has a safer paediatric profile; fluoroquinolones risk cartilage toxicity.
A child in a malaria‑endemic area has fever and diarrhoea. How do you rule out malaria as a cause? — Perform rapid malaria test; if positive, treat malaria and reassess diarrhoea aetiology.
What are the WHO criteria for severe dehydration and how do they guide fluid therapy? — ≥10 % weight loss, lethargy, weak pulse; requires IV Ringer’s lactate 100 ml/kg in 3 h.
Explain why normal serum sodium does not exclude dehydration in a child with diarrhoea. — Early dehydration may not yet alter serum sodium; clinical signs are more reliable.
What preventive strategies reduce gastroenteritis incidence in low‑resource settings? — Rotavirus vaccination, safe water, hand‑washing, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months.
ai.title: Acute Gastroenteritis in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Acute gastroenteritis is the commonest cause of diarrhoea and vomiting in children, especially in low‑resource settings. Diagnosis is clinical, severity is staged, and management focuses on rehydration, nutrition and treating the underlying pathogen when possible.

b: History of recent exposure to contaminated water, food, or sick contacts
Absence of blood in stool (unless dysentery)
No chronic diarrhoea (>14 days) or weight loss
sections.p: Acute gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the intestinal mucosa presenting with ≥3 loose stools or any vomiting within 14 days. Diagnosis is clinical; stool culture is reserved for severe or dysenteric cases.

t.b: Identifies bacterial or viral pathogen; guides antimicrobial use when positive
Detects HIV‑related diarrhoea; a positive result prompts ART evaluation

b: Some dehydration: ≥5 % weight loss, sunken eyes, thirst, skin pinch returns in 2–3 seconds
Severe dehydration: ≥10 % weight loss, lethargy, oliguria, weak pulse
sections.p: The WHO dehydration classification is used: no dehydration, some dehydration, and severe dehydration. This guides fluid therapy.

t.b: Assesses perfusion; >2 seconds suggests severe dehydration

b: Rotavirus – most common in children <2 years, seasonal peaks
Enterotoxigenic E. coli – linked to contaminated water
Shigella – dysentery with blood/mucus
Giardia lamblia – prolonged watery diarrhoea, often after untreated water
HIV infection – chronic diarrhoea, opportunistic pathogens
sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the common aetiologies are viral (rotavirus, norovirus), bacterial (enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shigella), and parasitic (Giardia, Cryptosporidium). Co‑factors such as HIV, malnutrition and recent antibiotic use increase risk.

b: 3–8 loose stools per day, may be profuse
Vomiting may precede diarrhoea
Fever <38.5 °C in viral disease, higher in bacterial infection
sections.p: Typical presentation includes sudden onset of watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low‑grade fever and abdominal cramps. Dehydration signs dominate the clinical picture.

b: Full blood count if fever >38.5 °C or suspected sepsis
Serum electrolytes only when severe dehydration or shock
sections.p: Investigations are guided by severity, duration and red‑flag features. In low‑resource settings, basic tests are prioritized.

t.b: Detects leukocytosis (bacterial infection) or anemia (chronic disease); if unavailable, rely on clinical fever and toxicity
Identifies hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia; if unavailable, monitor mental status and cardiac rhythm
Excludes malaria as a co‑cause of fever and diarrhoea

b: Severe dehydration or shock
Persistent vomiting >24 h preventing oral intake
Blood in stool or high‑grade fever (>39 °C)
Signs of sepsis: tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness
sections.p: Complications arise from profound dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and invasive bacterial infection.

b: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) 75 ml/kg over 4 h for some dehydration
IV Ringer’s lactate 100 ml/kg in 3 h for severe dehydration
Metronidazole 7‑10 days for Giardia – preferred over nitroimidazoles with poor safety profile
sections.p: Rehydration is the cornerstone; antimicrobial therapy is reserved for specific bacterial or parasitic aetiologies.

b: Review weight at 48 h; weight gain >5 % indicates adequate rehydration
Rotavirus vaccine (2‑dose schedule) for infants
Safe water, hand‑washing with soap, and proper food handling
sections.p: After rehydration, ensure return to normal stool frequency and weight gain. Preventive measures focus on hygiene and vaccination.

b: Acute appendicitis – localized right‑lower‑quadrant pain, fever, leukocytosis
Urinary tract infection – dysuria, flank pain, positive dipstick for nitrites
Intussusception – intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, “currant‑jelly” stool
sections.p: Conditions that mimic acute gastroenteritis must be considered to avoid missed diagnoses.

b: Normal stool microscopy does not exclude viral infection
Serum electrolytes may appear normal early in dehydration; clinical assessment remains key
sections.p: Certain investigations may be falsely reassuring or abnormal in this setting.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration (sunken eyes, lethargy, <5 ml/kg/h urine)
Blood in stool or high‑grade fever
